name: Magnesium deodorant

lead: Magnesium deodorants are a natural, aluminium-free way to keep underarms smelling fresh, using magnesium hydroxide, the active in milk of magnesia.

They work on odor, not sweat. Odor comes from bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat, and magnesium products are generally described as mildly alkaline odor reducers. Wikipedia's deodorant article notes milk of magnesia is sometimes used this way, and some versions contain trace sodium hypochlorite, a bactericide. No clinical studies were found.

paras: Applied to the underarms as a paste, cream or stick, in place of a conventional deodorant on a daily routine.
Magnesium hydroxide is labelled a mild skin, eye and respiratory irritant in bulk, and oral overuse can cause diarrhoea. No product-specific safety studies were found.

angle.text: Magnesium hydroxide deodorants, including milk of magnesia, are used as natural aluminium-free options for underarm odor. They are popular; no trials were found.

lead: Magnesium deodorant refers to aluminium-free deodorants built on a magnesium compound, most often magnesium hydroxide (the active in milk of magnesia), applied to the underarms to control odour.[1][2] People use them to smell clean and stay fresh, a basic part of how someone comes across, while avoiding aluminium-based antiperspirants.

Wikipedia's deodorant article notes that milk of magnesia is sometimes used this way, and that many versions contain a trace of sodium hypochlorite, a bactericide that may explain the bacteria-reducing effect.[1] Deodorants act on odour rather than on sweating: body odour arises when bacteria break down sweat secretions, and deodorants limit or mask this, whereas antiperspirants reduce sweating, usually with aluminium salts.[1][3]

Magnesium hydroxide is a poorly soluble white solid used mainly as an antacid and, in larger oral doses, a laxative.[2] Its deodorant use is lightly documented: the Wikipedia magnesium hydroxide article lists antiperspirant use without a supporting citation.[2] No clinical studies of magnesium deodorants were found.

paras: Products are sold as creams, sprays or pastes. Proponents present them as an alternative to aluminium-based antiperspirants and to baking soda deodorants, which can be irritating to some users.[1]

On T Nation, a 2010 thread on natural deodorants includes a poster who had heard of magnesium oil being used as a deodorant but had not tried it, and an older thread on antiperspirants includes the claim that aluminium inhibits magnesium absorption, which the poster offered as a reason for people taking magnesium supplements to reconsider antiperspirants.[4][5]

Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is produced industrially from seawater and is nearly insoluble in water.[2] Deodorants act on odour rather than sweat; body odour arises from bacterial breakdown of apocrine sweat secretions.[3] Magnesium hydroxide is mildly alkaline, and users and sellers describe magnesium products as odour-reducing; a verified mechanism for magnesium deodorants has not been published.

Wikipedia describes other natural options, including alum crystals (which still contain aluminium in a different salt form and can cause contact dermatitis in some people), activated charcoal and pH-neutral products.[1] On aluminium safety, it reports that the FDA in 2003 found data did not justify changing the status of aluminium antiperspirants, that a 2014 review of 469 studies found little evidence linking aluminium exposure to Alzheimer's, genetic damage or cancer, and that the US National Cancer Institute says no scientific evidence connects these products to breast cancer.[1]

Magnesium hydroxide carries a GHS warning for skin, eye and respiratory irritation.[2] Taken orally in large amounts it can cause diarrhoea, and long-term use may theoretically cause hypermagnesemia in kidney failure.[2] These warnings concern the bulk compound and oral use, not topical deodorants.

Fresh sweat is mostly odorless. Eccrine glands produce watery sweat, while apocrine glands in the armpits and groin produce oilier secretions containing proteins and fatty acids; skin bacteria break these down into smelly molecules [1][3]. Wikipedia names trans-3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid as a main odor source and describes Corynebacterium species as producing lipases that release odorous acids such as butyric acid, with Staphylococcus species adding thioalcohols and isovaleric acid [1][3]. Apocrine glands become active at puberty, which is when body odor typically begins [1].

The ABCC11 gene largely determines axillary odor: people with two copies of a loss-of-function variant produce less odor, and the variant is common among East Asians (80 to 95 percent) and rare in European and African populations (0 to 3 percent) [3]. Diet, gut microbiome and age also affect odor, and Wikipedia notes that a sweet or ammonia smell may sometimes signal a medical condition [3].

Deodorants control odor, whereas antiperspirants reduce sweat, usually with aluminum salts that form gel plugs in sweat ducts. In the US, deodorants are regulated as cosmetics and antiperspirants as drugs [1]. Wikipedia lists antimicrobials, fragrance masking and pH maintenance as the ways deodorants act, and notes that alkaline soaps raise skin pH and strip the acid mantle, which can make skin more hospitable to bacteria [1].

The first modern commercial deodorant, Mum, was patented in 1888 by Edna Murphey of Philadelphia; the first commercial antiperspirant, Everdry, appeared in 1903; and Helen Barnett Diserens's ball-point-pen-based applicator launched as Ban Roll-On in 1952 [1]. Between 1942 and 1957 the deodorant market grew about 600-fold, and by 1957 about half of men used deodorant [1].

Wikipedia's list of deodorant ingredient types includes aluminum salts, alum, antibacterials such as triclosan, pH-neutral products, fragrance and essential oils, activated charcoal and milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide), the last used less often, with some versions containing trace sodium hypochlorite [1]. Magnesium hydroxide is mildly alkaline. In commercial natural deodorants it is typically combined with other ingredients such as plant oils, and users describe it as gentler than baking soda, which can irritate some skin.

Early deodorants used zinc oxide, ammonium chloride, sodium bicarbonate and formaldehyde, the last now considered a carcinogen [1]. Magnesium-based products belong to the modern wave of aluminum-free and natural formulations.

Wikipedia reports that propylene glycol can irritate skin, alum crystals are a weak irritant, and zirconium can cause granulomas [1]. Sprays held too close to the skin can cause cold burns [1]. The FDA warns people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminum antiperspirants [1]. Because magnesium deodorants are deodorants, not antiperspirants, they do not reduce sweat, and users who want less wetness would look at other product categories.
